chapter_theme: Three songs at Thilathaippathi (திலதைப்பதி): a short plea not to be tossed by impurity and maya, a confession of wandering in waves of pleasure addressed to the Lord who knows it, and a plea to stop singing the praise of men and sing his; the praise includes the rescue of the elephant Gajendra.
structure_note: 802 is a four-line song on malam and maya; 803 confesses lovemaking without an explicit plea; 804 sets Kama's arrows against the poet's praise and turns from praise of the world.

802.reading: In a short song the poet asks whether he must be tossed about by impurity and maya, too great to tell, through a life that is a mere moment and even that a time of eating from a leaf. The praise names the vel that ended the imprisonment of the gods kept in the great jail, at Thilathaippathi.
802.nuance: இறை அத்தனையோ ... இலையிட்டு உணல் ஏய்தரு காலம்: the life span may be called 'only a moment' and taken up with eating; the opening lines are compressed and the sense is a guess. அறையில் பெரிதாம் மலமாயை names impurity and maya together, a Siddhanta pairing.

803.reading: The poet describes the women whose breasts, like a serpent's hood, bear pearl strings and gold, with cloud-dark hair full of flowers, swan's gait and a parrot's sweet speech, and says that, his heart burning without pity, his mind deluded, he embraces them and wanders in the waves of pleasure; he says this to the Lord 'who knows it always' and makes no further plea. The praise has Murugan come to the sound of the drum, given in the metre's own syllables (தனனத் தனன தந்த, தகிடத் தகிட), at Thilathaippathi of red paddy, lotus, sugarcane and a tall peak.
803.nuance: The plea is replaced by a statement: திரிவன் என்று அறிவோனே, 'you who know that I wander so'. Lines 9 and 10 set out the song's metrical pattern (தனனத் தனன தந்த ... தனதானா) as the drum's sound, and the next line continues it as the beat of the drum.

804.reading: The poet asks whether, freed from the eyes that dart toward the makara earrings with enchanting arrows, from breasts that outdo Meru and the sandal pot, and from Kama's flower arrows that torment a trembling body and a heart in the furnace of longing, and rid of the babble of praising the world, he will wander speaking the praise that is rightfully Murugan's. The praise tells how the elephant entered the lotus pool, was seized by the crocodile and stood struggling and bewildered, and how Vishnu, the boon-giver, came at once as its refuge and threw the discus; Murugan is the son of Siva's consort, born of the same body as that Vishnu, at Thilathaippathi where Siva's devotees, the freed, gods, ascetics and siddhas gather with one mind.
804.nuance: உலகப் புகழ் புலம்பு கலி அற்று ... உன் உரிமைப் புகழ் பகர்ந்து: the poet sets the praise of worldly men against the praise that belongs to Murugan, a turn his songs at the court shrines make often. The praise tells the story of Gajendra in its unmistakable details (the pool, the crocodile, the discus). Uma is called Vishnu's sister (வரதற்கு உடற்பிறந்த சிவை).

links.note: 804 asks to be rid of the babble of praising the world (உலகப் புகழ்ப் புலம்பு கலி அற்று) and to speak the praise that is rightfully Murugan's (உன் உரிமைப் புகழ்), and its praise tells how Vishnu saved the elephant from the crocodile. 292 quotes the patron-poem it renounces, in which a poor man was likened even to the god who helped in the crocodile pool (முதலை மடுவினில் அதவிய புயல்). The same story is spent on a patron in one song and kept for the god's own praise in the other.
